Classical

/KLASS-ih-kuhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Classical means relating to a traditional, long-established style or form, especially one regarded as a standard of excellence, such as ancient Greek and Roman culture.

The architect designed the new courthouse in a classical style, with tall columns and a triangular pediment echoing ancient Rome.

Worked Example

Rather than composing an entirely modern score, the film's composer chose a classical structure for the main theme — a full orchestra, a clear melodic line, and formal movements — deliberately evoking symphonies written two centuries earlier.

The composer wasn't inventing a brand-new musical form; he was drawing on a long-established tradition treated as a model of excellence, which is exactly what "classical" describes.

How Classical Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

traditional

traditional: emphasizes long-established custom generally, not specifically ancient Greek/Roman style

time-honored

time-honored: stresses respect earned through long use over time

canonical

canonical: suggests something treated as an official model or standard

Antonyms

modern

modern: belonging to the present or recent era, rather than tradition

avant-garde

avant-garde: experimental and ahead of its time, the opposite of established tradition

How Strong Is It? — traditional → time-honored → classical

traditional vs. classical

traditional vs. classical: A traditional recipe has simply been passed down through a family or culture.

time-honored vs. classical

time-honored vs. classical: Time-honored is weaker than classical: a time-honored recipe has earned respect by surviving, but a classical form goes further, standing as the very standard of excellence others are measured against.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of classical.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — class-

Root — class-: a group or division (Latin classis)

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: relating to — this much on its own already spells a word: classic

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: relating to, again — a second adjective ending layered on top of classic, which is already a word on its own. English pairs -ic and -al so often that -ical reads as a single familiar ending (historic/historical, comic/comical), and where both forms survive the longer one is usually the more specialised of the two.

Put it together

Put it together: "Classical" builds on class-, originally referring to a defined social rank; over time, the "classical" writers and artists of ancient Greece and Rome came to represent the top, most esteemed rank of cultural achievement — hence "classical" now means belonging to that standard-setting tradition.

Use the root in a new word: classify

Use the root in a new word: classify: Librarians classify each new book by subject before shelving it.
